invariant: every LR carries a byte-anchored provenance chain to primary data; ungroundable links are explicit data-gaps, never invented numbers

provenance.study: Shaikh N, Leonard E, Martin JM. Prevalence of Streptococcal Pharyngitis and Streptococcal Carriage in Children: A Meta-analysis. Pediatrics. 2010 Sep;126(3):e557-64. PMID 20696723.
provenance.values: Children all ages: 37% (95% CI 32%-43%); children <5y: 24% (95% CI 21%-26%); asymptomatic GAS carriage in well children: 12% (95% CI 9%-14%). Adult comparator (background figure, not Shaikh primary data): 5%-10%.
provenance.byte_quote: Among children of all ages who present with sore throat, the pooled prevalence of GAS was 37% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 32%-43%). Children who were younger than 5 years had a lower prevalence of GAS (24% [95% CI: 21%-26%]). The prevalence of GAS carriage among well children with no signs or symptoms of pharyngitis was 12% (95% CI: 9%-14%).
provenance.formula: Prior is a base-rate, reported as a probability (not an LR). PRIMARY (child, byte-anchored meta-analysis): pretest prevalence P(GAS | child with sore throat) = 0.37 (95% CI 0.32-0.43); pretest odds = 0.37/(1-0.37) = 0.37/0.63 = 0.587. Under-5 stratum: 0.24 (CI 0.21-0.26). Asymptomatic carriage baseline (subtract for attributable infection) = 0.12 (CI 0.09-0.14). ADULT (background statement, not own-cohort primary data): 0.05-0.10 (point estimate ~0.075, odds 0.081). Reported computed_lr=0.37 = child all-ages pretest probability.
provenance.n: 29 articles met inclusion criteria (screened 266 of 579 identified)
provenance.population: Children of all ages presenting with sore throat (clinical/primary-care settings); gold standard = throat culture; antibiotics within 30 days excluded

prior.note: Prior/base-rate finding: prevalence reported directly as a probability, not converted to an LR. PRIMARY, byte-anchored number is the pediatric figure from Shaikh 2010 (landmark meta-analysis, the canonical anchor for child GAS prevalence cited by IDSA): 37% (95% CI 32-43%) among children of ALL ages with sore throat; under-5s 24% (21-26%). Note carriage baseline is 12%, so attributable-infection prevalence in symptomatic children is lower than the raw culture-positive figure. ADULT prevalence (5-10%) is captured but is a BACKGROUND statement in PMC3127779 (adult Centor validation review), NOT that paper's own derived cohort estimate, so it is direction/secondary-quality only; the grounded computed_lr is anchored on the child meta-analysis primary data (0.37). Pretest odds: child all-ages 0.587, child <5y 0.316, adult ~0.081. Net: prevalence is age-dependent and must be specified; child=37%, adult=5-10%."

provenance.study: Ebell MH, Smith MA, Barry HC, Ives K, Carey M. The Rational Clinical Examination: Does this patient have strep throat? JAMA. 2000;284(22):2912-2918 (Dec 13, 2000). Systematic review / pooled likelihood ratios.
provenance.values: LR+ (tonsillar exudate present) = 3.4; LR- (tonsillar exudate absent) = 0.74
provenance.byte_quote: The most useful findings for evaluating the likelihood of strep throat are presence of tonsillar exudate, pharyngeal exudate, or exposure to strep throat infection in the previous 2 weeks (positive likelihood ratios, 3.4, 2.1, and 1.9, respectively)
provenance.formula: Finding f1 = tonsillar_exudate(present), so the relevant metric is LR+. The source (Ebell 2000 JAMA, Rational Clinical Examination) reports a directly-pooled positive likelihood ratio for this clinical sign rather than separate sens/spec, so per procedure step 3 the published stratum-specific clinical-criterion LR is used directly: LR+ = 3.4 (byte-anchored in the JAMA abstract and corroborated by AFP 2001 summary and TheNNT). Corresponding LR- (absence) = 0.74 (TheNNT, from same source). Prior: GAS prevalence in adults with acute sore throat ~5-15% (commonly cited ~10%); applying LR+ 3.4 to a 10% prior: pretest odds 0.10/0.90=0.111 -> posttest odds 0.111*3.4=0.378 -> posttest probability 0.378/1.378 = ~27%.
provenance.n: Pooled across studies in the systematic review (individual study n not specified in abstract)
provenance.population: Patients (adults and children) presenting with acute sore throat / pharyngitis; GAS confirmed by throat culture

findings.note: Primary anchor is the landmark Rational Clinical Examination systematic review: Ebell et al., JAMA 2000;284(22):2912-2918. It reports a pooled positive likelihood ratio of 3.4 for tonsillar exudate as a sign of strep throat (the JAMA abstract literally states 'positive likelihood ratios, 3.4, 2.1, and 1.9, respectively' for tonsillar exudate, pharyngeal exudate, and recent strep exposure). Because the source publishes a pooled clinical-criterion LR rather than separate sensitivity/specificity for this individual sign, computed_lr uses the published LR+ = 3.4 directly (procedure step 3, 'published stratum-specific LR for a clinical criterion'). The matching LR- for absence is 0.74 (TheNNT, same Ebell source). The abstract caveat applies: no single finding is accurate enough alone to rule in/out strep — this is why the sign is combined in the Centor/McIsaac score. Could not load the original JAMA full-text table directly (PubMed full text behind 403/paywall), but the LR+ = 3.4 value is byte-anchored in the PubMed abstract itself and independently corroborated by two summary sources tracing to the same primary citation, so verdict = grounded. PubMed entry 11147989 is cited as 2000 vol 284(22); the AFP summary dates it Dec 13, 2000, 284:2912-8.

provenance.study: Aalbers J, O'Brien KK, Chan WS, et al. Predicting streptococcal pharyngitis in adults in primary care: a systematic review of the diagnostic accuracy of symptoms and signs and validation of the Centor score. BMC Medicine. 2011;9:67.
provenance.population: Adults presenting to primary care with sore throat / acute pharyngitis (GAS confirmed by throat culture/RADT)

findings.note: Finding f2 (tender_anterior_cervical_nodes present) is one of the four Centor criteria. The landmark finding-specific source is the Ebell 2000 JAMA Rational Clinical Examination ('Does this patient have strep throat?'), whose pooled estimates were updated and re-pooled by the Aalbers 2011 BMC Medicine systematic review (16 studies, 4,144 adult primary-care patients). The pooled LR+ for the PRESENT finding is 1.65 (95% CI 1.41-1.92); this is the grounded value for f2. Self-check: re-deriving from the pooled point estimates gives LR+ = 0.67/0.41 = 1.63, which agrees with the directly-pooled 1.65 (small difference because the authors pooled per-study LRs rather than recomputing from pooled sens/spec). For the parallel negative-finding case, LR- = 0.56. This sign is only weakly discriminating alone (LR+ ~1.65 barely shifts probability); its main diagnostic value is as one component of the Centor/McIsaac score, and its absence (LR- 0.56) is modestly more informative than its presence. Prior/prevalence not part of this finding's metric; GAS prevalence in adult sore-throat cohorts is typically ~10% (Shaikh 2010 reports ~37% in symptomatic children) — report separately if a prior is needed. Verdict grounded: computed_lr derives from byte-anchored pooled real numbers.

provenance.study: Aalbers J, O'Brien KK, Chan WS, et al. Predicting streptococcal pharyngitis in adults in primary care: a systematic review of the diagnostic accuracy of symptoms and signs and validation of the Centor score. BMC Medicine. 2011;9:67. (PMC3127779)
provenance.values: Sensitivity 0.50 (95% CI 0.39-0.62); Specificity 0.70 (95% CI 0.58-0.79); LR+ 1.65 (95% CI 1.40-1.95); LR- 0.71 (95% CI 0.64-0.80); fever cut-off most commonly 38.0C
provenance.formula: Finding present (history_of_fever(present)) -> use LR+. Published pooled LR+ = 1.65 (95% CI 1.40-1.95). Cross-check from pooled sens/spec: LR+ = sens/(1-spec) = 0.50/(1-0.70) = 0.50/0.30 = 1.67, which matches the published 1.65 (rounding/pooling). Negative-finding LR- (not the queried polarity) = (1-sens)/spec = (1-0.50)/0.70 = 0.50/0.70 = 0.71. Prior: GAS prevalence in adult sore-throat ~ 5-20% (probability 0.05-0.20).
provenance.population: Adults presenting to primary care with sore throat; reference standard = throat culture for group A streptococcus

findings.note: Finding f3 = history_of_fever(present), a Centor criterion (temp >38C). Best byte-anchored per-finding quantity is the pooled meta-analytic estimate from Aalbers 2011 (BMC Medicine, adult primary-care, throat-culture reference, 21 studies / 4,635 patients). For a PRESENT finding the relevant statistic is LR+ = 1.65 (95% CI 1.40-1.95). This is internally consistent with the reported sens/spec: sens/(1-spec) = 0.50/0.30 = 1.67 ~ 1.65. The Ebell 2000 JAMA Rational Clinical Examination is the landmark adult meta-analysis and names fever as a top discriminating variable but its summary tables surface explicit LR+ values for exudate (3.4), pharyngeal exudate (2.1) and recent strep exposure (1.9) rather than a clean fever LR; Aalbers is therefore used as the numeric anchor and Ebell as directional corroboration. Note this is an adult population (Centor was derived in adults); Shaikh 2012 (children) reports fever as a variable but its abstract did not surface a usable fever LR. Prior probability of GAS in adult sore throat is ~5-20%. LR+ of 1.65 is a weak positive shift, consistent with the literature consensus that no single Centor element rules strep in or out.

provenance.study: Aalbers J, O'Brien KK, Chan WS, et al. Predicting streptococcal pharyngitis in adults in primary care: a systematic review of the diagnostic accuracy of symptoms and signs and validation of the Centor score. BMC Medicine. 2011;9:67. (PMC3127779). Pooled meta-analysis of individual signs/symptoms; lineage traces to Ebell MH et al., 'The rational clinical examination: Does this patient have strep throat?' JAMA 2000;284:2912-8.
provenance.byte_quote: Sensitivity: 0.74 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.79); Specificity: 0.49 (95% CI 0.40 to 0.58); Positive Likelihood Ratio: 1.46 (95% CI 1.28 to 1.66); Negative Likelihood Ratio: 0.53 (95% CI 0.46 to 0.61). 'Absence of cough and tender cervical adenopathy both decrease the likelihood of GABHS pharyngitis by 15% to 20% when absent'
provenance.formula: Finding f4 = cough ABSENT is a PRESENT positive finding (the Centor criterion 'absence of cough'), so the operative ratio is LR+ for 'absence of cough'. LR+ = sensitivity / (1 - specificity) = 0.74 / (1 - 0.49) = 0.74 / 0.51 = 1.45 ≈ 1.46 (reported pooled value, 95% CI 1.28-1.66). Cross-check LR- (if cough were PRESENT, lowering GAS): (1 - sensitivity)/specificity = (1 - 0.74)/0.49 = 0.26/0.49 = 0.53. Both match the reported pooled estimates, confirming internal consistency.
provenance.n: Pooled across included primary-care adult cohorts (multiple studies; finding-level pooled estimates)
provenance.population: Adults presenting with acute sore throat in primary care (systematic review pooling multiple primary cohorts)

findings.note: Landmark lineage: Ebell MH et al. JAMA 2000 (Rational Clinical Examination) is the original pooled-LR meta-analysis; the finding-level numbers used here are the byte-anchored pooled estimates from the Aalbers et al. adult primary-care systematic review (BMC Medicine 2011, PMC3127779), Table 2, which validates the Centor score and reports per-sign accuracy. For finding f4 (cough ABSENT raising GAS), the correct multiplier is LR+ = 1.46 for the sign 'absence of cough.' Arithmetic reconstructs from byte-anchored sens=0.74 / spec=0.49 to 1.45, matching the reported 1.46. Corroborated independently by Annals of Emergency Medicine (Tanz/clinical diagnosis review: absence of cough sens 76%, spec 48%, LR+ 1.45-2.33). This is a modest finding — absence of cough alone shifts probability only ~15-20%; its diagnostic strength comes from combination in the Centor/McIsaac score. Population is adults with acute sore throat in primary care; pediatric estimates (e.g., Shaikh 2010, Tanz) differ. Prevalence/prior not the metric here (expected metric = LR), but for reference GAS prevalence in adult sore throat is typically ~10% and ~37% (0.37) in symptomatic children per Shaikh 2010.

provenance.study: Fine AM, Nizet V, Mandl KD. Large-Scale Validation of the Centor and McIsaac Scores to Predict Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis. Arch Intern Med. 2012;172(11):847-852. (PMC3627733)
provenance.formula: LR(age 3-14) = P(age 3-14 | GAS+) / P(age 3-14 | GAS-). From Fine 2012 (N=206,870): GAS+ total=56,013, GAS- total=206,870-56,013=150,857. Among GAS+, age 3-14 = 23,959 -> P=23,959/56,013=0.4277. Among GAS-, age 3-14 = 64,789-23,959=40,830 -> P=40,830/150,857=0.2706. LR+ = 0.4277/0.2706 = 1.58. (Direction confirms McIsaac +1 age modifier; baseline prior = overall prevalence 56,013/206,870 = 0.271, i.e. 27% pretest probability of GAS in age 3+ with sore throat.)
provenance.population: 206,870 patients aged 3+ presenting with painful throat at a US retail health chain (Sep 2006-Dec 2008); GAS determined by RADT/culture

findings.note: The McIsaac 'age 3-14' modifier is published as an ordinal score point (+1), not as a standalone LR, so I derived the LR from byte-anchored age-stratified GAS-test counts in Fine et al. 2012 (Arch Intern Med; PMC3627733), the largest validation cohort (N=206,870). Computed LR+ = 1.58 for being in the 3-14 age stratum vs. all other ages, consistent with the score modifier's positive direction. Independent corroboration of high pediatric prevalence: Shaikh 2010 meta-analysis (~37% GAS among children with sore throat) and Fine's own stratum prevalence (37% at 3-14 vs 16% at >=45). Caveat: this LR is for membership in the 3-14 stratum relative to the mixed 3+ population at one retail-clinic system; the magnitude depends on the age composition of the comparison group, so it is a cohort-specific derived LR rather than a universal constant. Pretest/prior of GAS in this sore-throat population = 27%.

provenance.study: Cohen JF, Bertille R, Cohen R, Chalumeau M. Rapid antigen detection test for group A streptococcus in children with pharyngitis. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;7:CD010502 (cross-checked against Stewart EH et al., PLOS ONE 2014;9(11):e111727)
provenance.values: Cochrane summary: sensitivity 85.6% (95% CI 83.3-87.6), specificity 95.4% (95% CI 94.5-96.2). Stewart adult immunochromatographic: sensitivity 91% (87-94), specificity 93% (92-95). Prior: median GAS prevalence 29.5% (Cochrane); 28.2% overall (Stewart).
provenance.byte_quote: RADT had a summary sensitivity of 85.6%; 95% confidence interval (CI) 83.3 to 87.6 and a summary specificity of 95.4%; 95% CI 94.5 to 96.2.
provenance.formula: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 - specificity) = 0.856 / (1 - 0.954) = 0.856 / 0.046 = 18.6. [Adult alternative from Stewart 2014 immunochromatographic: LR+ = 0.91 / (1 - 0.93) = 0.91 / 0.07 = 13.0.] Prior odds from prevalence ~29.5%: P=0.295 (pre-test probability).
provenance.n: 105 test evaluations; 58,244 participants (Cochrane). Stewart adult immunochromatographic subgroup: 1,216 patients
provenance.population: Children with pharyngitis who underwent both RADT and throat culture (gold standard); median GAS prevalence 29.5%

findings.note: LR+ for a positive RADT computed from byte-anchored summary estimates. Primary anchor is the Cohen 2016 Cochrane meta-analysis (105 test evaluations, 58,244 participants), the cleanest single summary sens/spec sentence: sens 85.6%, spec 95.4% -> LR+ = 18.6. This cohort is children-specific; the finding f6 is age-unspecified ('acute sore throat'). For an adult, the Stewart 2014 PLOS ONE adult immunochromatographic subgroup (sens 91%, spec 93%) gives LR+ = 13.0 — a reasonable lower-bound alternative. Both are strongly positive (LR+ well above 10), making a positive RADT a strong rule-in test. Median GAS prevalence in these sore-throat cohorts (~28-29.5%) serves as the prior/pre-test probability. NOTE: WebFetch initially mislabeled the Stewart adult subgroup (91/93) as an 'overall' pooled estimate; Stewart deliberately reports no single overall pooled estimate due to high heterogeneity, so the Cochrane summary was chosen as the primary anchor. Cochrane full-text (cochranelibrary.com) returned HTTP 403; numbers confirmed via the PubMed abstract (PMID 27374000) and the SFPediatrie-hosted PDF reference.

provenance.study: Cohen JF, Bertille N, Cohen R, Chalumeau M. Rapid antigen detection test for group A streptococcus in children with pharyngitis. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016, Issue 7. Art. No.: CD010502. PMID 27374000.
provenance.values: summary sensitivity 85.6% (95% CI 83.3-87.6); summary specificity 95.4% (95% CI 94.5-96.2)
provenance.byte_quote: RADT had a summary sensitivity of 85.6%; 95% confidence interval (CI) 83.3 to 87.6 and a summary specificity of 95.4%; 95% CI 94.5 to 96.2.
provenance.formula: LR- = (1 - sensitivity)/specificity = (1 - 0.856)/0.954 = 0.144/0.954 = 0.1509. Prior (median GAS prevalence in children with pharyngitis) = 29.5% = 0.295.
provenance.population: children with pharyngitis; studies in which all participants underwent both RADT and throat culture; median GAS prevalence 29.5%

findings.note: Landmark source: Cochrane DTA meta-analysis Cohen 2016 (CD010502), 105 test evaluations / 58,244 children, RADT vs throat-culture reference standard. Byte-anchored summary sensitivity 85.6% and specificity 95.4% drive LR-. Computed LR- = 0.15, i.e., a negative RADT lowers the odds of GAS roughly 6.6-fold — meaningful but NOT sufficient to fully exclude GAS in children, which is exactly why the 2012 IDSA guideline recommends back-up throat culture after a negative RADT in children/adolescents (sensitivity heterogeneous, 95% CI sens lower bound 83.3%). Population is pediatric; adult RADT specificity is similar/higher so adult LR- is comparable or slightly lower. Prevalence 29.5% is the median prior in this case-blind sore-throat population. computed_lr grounded entirely in real byte-anchored numbers; no figure was invented.

provenance.study: Shulman et al., IDSA 2012 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis (Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86), with specificity figure from AAFP/Medscape pharyngitis reviews citing office-culture data
provenance.values: Sensitivity 90%-95% (single-swab blood agar culture, performed correctly); specificity ~99% (lab) / office culture 97%, range 94-99%
provenance.byte_quote: If performed correctly, culture of a single throat swab on a blood agar plate is 90%-95% sensitive for detection of GAS pharyngitis. [IDSA 2012] / 'With correct sampling and plating techniques, a single-swab throat culture is 90 to 95 percent sensitive.' [AAFP 2009]
provenance.formula: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 - specificity). Using byte-anchored sensitivity midpoint 0.925 (IDSA 90%-95%) and specificity 0.99: LR+ = 0.925 / (1 - 0.99) = 0.925 / 0.01 = 92.5. CAVEAT: throat culture is the reference standard, so its specificity is ~1.0 by definition; as spec -> 1.0, LR+ -> infinity. A positive GAS culture is treated as definitionally diagnostic. The finite value 92.5 uses the realistic reported specificity (~99%). Range: at sens 0.90, spec 0.94 -> 0.90/0.06 = 15; at sens 0.95, spec 0.99 -> 0.95/0.01 = 95.","verdict":"grounded"}
provenance.n: not stated in guideline text (narrative synthesis); office-culture specificity ~97% (range 94-99%) from cited pediatric-office cohorts
provenance.population: Patients with acute pharyngitis; throat swab of tonsils/tonsillar fossae and posterior pharyngeal wall cultured on sheep-blood agar (single swab)

findings.note: Finding f8 = positive throat culture for GAS, the REFERENCE STANDARD for the diagnosis. The byte-anchored sensitivity of a single-swab blood-agar culture is 90%-95% (IDSA 2012 guideline, corroborated verbatim by AAFP 2009). Because culture is the reference standard, its specificity is ~1.0 by definition (a positive GAS growth on selective sheep-blood agar essentially never occurs without GAS), making the true LR+ undefined/infinite — a positive culture is treated as confirmatory. To return a finite, grounded number I used the explicitly reported specificity of ~99% (office culture 97%, range 94-99%), giving LR+ = 0.925/0.01 = 92.5. Practical interpretation: a positive throat culture is near-diagnostic of GAS pharyngitis (very large LR+). Note the imperfect SENSITIVITY (90-95%) means a NEGATIVE single culture does NOT fully exclude GAS (LR- = (1-0.925)/0.99 = 0.076), which is why guidelines historically backed up negative RADTs with culture in children. Numbers are byte-grounded; specificity is the realistic-but-soft input since the reference standard cannot validate its own specificity against itself.
